# Purpose of this guide

This document is intended to become a living, cohort-built guide to measuring melatonin in human circadian research. It combines the course timetable, a common reading core, individual student literature assignments, and a structured protocol framework that can be refined during the week. The emphasis is not simply on learning how to collect saliva samples. By the end of the course, the guide should make explicit how participant preparation, light exposure, food and substances, posture, biological specimen, sample timing, pre-analytics, assay choice, DLMO calculation, metadata and quality control can each change the meaning of a melatonin profile. The course runs from Monday, 14 September to Friday, 18 September 2026 at the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics in Tübingen. Evening data collection is built around repeated melatonin measurements from 18:00 to 00:00 on Monday through Thursday.

# How the living document works

Each participant owns one section of the guide. Before the course, the assigned student should use the seed literature below as a starting point, extend the search independently, and prepare a concise evidence synthesis. During the course, each section will be revised in light of the practical data collection and group discussion. By Friday, the goal is to convert the literature summaries into concrete recommendations for a reproducible melatonin protocol. The student sections should therefore answer a methodological question, not simply summarize papers. Statements should distinguish evidence from convention, identify uncertainty, and end with a recommendation about what should be standardized, measured, documented or reported.

## Student contribution and presentation requirements

The following limits keep the contributions comparable and make it possible to integrate all 19 sections into one guide.

| Component | Requirement |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Written contribution | **Maximum 600 words**, excluding references |
| Literature | **5-8 references total**, including the seed literature; at least **2 additional papers** found independently |
| Evidence mix | Include primary evidence and, where useful, a methodological paper or review |
| Protocol recommendation | End with a **maximum 80-word** practical recommendation |
| Oral presentation | **5 minutes** plus **1 minute** for a question or clarification |
| Slides | Up to **3 content slides**, plus one references slide if needed |
| Referencing | Provide DOI and PMID whenever available; if one identifier is unavailable, provide the identifier that is available |

The 600-word preparatory contribution is separate from the course's 2000-word assessed report.

# Course schedule

The afternoon and evening structure is designed around lectures beginning at 16:00 and repeated melatonin sampling from 18:00 to 00:00. Friday is reserved for student presentations, synthesis and completion of the living guide, with the course ending by 12:00.

| Day | Teaching | Melatonin sampling | Main purpose |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Monday, 14 September | From 16:00: course introduction; melatonin physiology; DLMO; practical sampling setup | **18:00-00:00, every 30 minutes (13 planned samples)** | Learn the collection workflow and establish consistent documentation |
| Tuesday, 15 September | From 16:00: sampling matrices, pre-analytics, food/substance effects and assays | **18:00-00:00, every 30 minutes (13 planned samples)** | Connect practical sampling decisions to pre-analytical and analytical validity |
| Wednesday, 16 September | From 16:00: biological and behavioral modifiers; quality control | **18:00-00:00, every 30 minutes (13 planned samples)** | Examine standardization, deviations and biological variability |
| Thursday, 17 September | From 16:00: light, prior light history, DLMO analysis, reproducibility and synthesis | **18:00-00:00, every 30 minutes (13 planned samples)** | Link sampling, exposure measurement and phase estimation |
| Friday, 18 September | **09:00-11:30 student presentations and integration; 11:30-12:00 final synthesis and close** | No evening collection | Convert the week's evidence and experience into the final guide |

# Common framework for every melatonin collection evening

The final guide should make every evening traceable from participant state through assay result. At minimum, each sampling night should capture the session identifier, actual clock time of every sample, any deviation from schedule, the light environment, relevant food and substance exposure, posture and activity, the biological specimen and collection device, sample handling and storage, assay method and batch, and the rule used to derive DLMO or other phase markers. The same metadata structure should be used across all four nights so that biological differences can be separated from changes in measurement practice.

::: callout-important
## Sampling schedule

Melatonin samples are collected **every 30 minutes from 18:00 through 00:00**, giving **13 planned samples per participant per evening**: 18:00, 18:30, 19:00, 19:30, 20:00, 20:30, 21:00, 21:30, 22:00, 22:30, 23:00, 23:30 and 00:00. The planned and actual collection time should both be recorded so that deviations are visible during analysis.
:::

# Foundations and phase estimation

## Melatonin physiology, circadian phase and the DLMO concept

**Assigned student:** Carolina Guidolin

Establish what endogenous melatonin is, why its evening rise is useful as a circadian phase marker, and what DLMO does and does not measure. Distinguish circadian phase from melatonin concentration or amplitude, and explain why a full time series is more informative than a single sample.

The section should resolve three practical questions:

-   What physiological process generates the nocturnal melatonin rhythm?
-   Why is DLMO used as a marker of central circadian phase?
-   Which conclusions can and cannot be drawn from DLMO timing and melatonin amplitude?

**Protocol contribution:** Define the conceptual interpretation that should accompany every DLMO estimate in the final guide.

### Seed literature

-   Benloucif S et al. Measuring melatonin in humans. *Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine*. 2008. DOI: [10.5664/jcsm.27083](https://doi.org/10.5664/jcsm.27083). PMID: 18350967.
-   St Hilaire MA, Lockley SW. Measuring Dim Light Melatonin Onset in Humans. *Methods in Molecular Biology*. 2022. DOI: [10.1007/978-1-0716-2593-4_3](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-0716-2593-4_3). PMID: 36180672.
-   Lockley SW. Journal of Pineal Research guideline for authors: Measuring melatonin in humans. *Journal of Pineal Research*. 2020. DOI: [10.1111/jpi.12664](https://doi.org/10.1111/jpi.12664). PMID: 32344453.

### Student contribution

Students should write this section using the structure below. **The complete contribution must remain within 600 words, excluding references.** Synthesize across studies rather than summarizing papers one by one. Where the evidence is inconsistent or weak, say so explicitly.

#### Evidence synthesis

**Suggested length: 250-300 words.** Summarize what the literature collectively shows about the assigned topic. Focus on findings that affect the validity, interpretation or practical conduct of melatonin measurement. Compare studies where relevant and distinguish well-supported findings from common practice or convention.

#### Sources of variability and uncertainty

**Suggested length: 100-150 words.** Identify the main biological, behavioral, technical or analytical factors that could explain variation between participants, studies or methods. Note important limitations, unresolved questions and situations in which the available evidence may not generalize.

#### Implications for measurement and reporting

**Suggested length: 100-150 words.** Translate the evidence into consequences for study design and conduct. State what researchers should control, standardize, measure, document or report, and explain briefly why these elements matter.

#### Protocol recommendation

**Maximum 80 words.** Give a concise recommendation that can be incorporated directly into the final cohort melatonin protocol. It should be specific enough to act on and should distinguish requirements supported by evidence from pragmatic choices that simply need to be standardized within a study.

#### References

Provide **5-8 references in total**, including the seed literature and at least **2 additional papers identified independently**. Include DOI and PMID whenever available, with the DOI formatted as a clickable link.

## Sampling window, sampling frequency and DLMO threshold

**Assigned student:** Gabriel Agbeshie

Examine how the timing and frequency of samples affect DLMO estimation. Compare fixed and relative threshold approaches, consider low secretors and incomplete profiles, and identify the trade-off between burden, assay cost and phase-estimation precision.

The section should resolve three practical questions:

-   How early before expected DLMO should sampling begin and how long should it continue?
-   What is lost when sampling is hourly rather than every 30 minutes?
-   How should thresholds, interpolation and failed DLMO estimates be documented?

**Protocol contribution:** Recommend a sampling-window and analysis rule set, while clearly identifying what remains study-specific.

### Seed literature

-   Molina TA, Burgess HJ. Calculating the dim light melatonin onset: the impact of threshold and sampling rate. *Chronobiology International*. 2011. DOI: [10.3109/07420528.2011.597531](https://doi.org/10.3109/07420528.2011.597531). PMID: 21823817.

## Sleep timing, chronotype and phase angle

**Assigned student:** Lorna Caddick

# Biological specimens and collection setting

## Salivary melatonin collection and pre-analytics

**Assigned student:** Nicole Needham

Develop the practical section on saliva collection. Cover passive drool versus collection devices, oral contamination, sample volume, collection duration, labeling, immediate handling, storage, freeze-thaw considerations and documentation of deviations. Emphasize how pre-analytical choices can interact with the assay.

The section should resolve three practical questions:

-   Which collection devices are suitable for low salivary melatonin concentrations?
-   What should participants avoid or document around sample collection?
-   Which collection, handling and storage metadata are needed for reproducibility?

**Protocol contribution:** Produce the step-by-step saliva collection standard and deviation log for the living guide.

**Assigned student:** Özgun Yetkin

Review blood-based melatonin measurement, including total versus free melatonin, plasma versus serum, repeated venous sampling, sample handling and the relationship between blood and saliva concentrations. Compare scientific advantages with participant burden and practical complexity.

The section should resolve three practical questions:

-   What does blood measurement offer that saliva does not?
-   How closely do salivary and plasma melatonin track one another?

**Protocol contribution:** Define when blood sampling is justified and which collection and processing variables must be reported.

## Urinary melatonin and 6-sulphatoxymelatonin (aMT6s)

**Assigned student:** Maria Oertel

Explain urinary measurement of the principal melatonin metabolite 6-sulphatoxymelatonin, including timed collections, normalization or excretion-rate approaches, and how urine differs from saliva or plasma as a marker of circadian timing and integrated melatonin production.

# Analytical methods

## Radioimmunoassay (RIA) for melatonin

**Assigned student:** Lucien Bickerstaff

Explain the principles, historical importance, analytical strengths and limitations of radioimmunoassay for melatonin. Address extraction, sensitivity, specificity, cross-reactivity, calibration, quality control and the practical consequences of using radioactive tracers.

The section should resolve three practical questions:

-   How does RIA quantify melatonin and why was it historically important?
-   What are the main sources of analytical bias or imprecision?
-   Which validation characteristics must be reported before results can be compared across assays?

**Protocol contribution:** Define the assay-performance information that a paper or dataset using RIA should report.

### Seed literature

-   Kennaway DJ et al. A specific radioimmunoassay for melatonin in biological tissue and fluids and its validation by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. *Endocrinology*. 1977. DOI: [10.1210/endo-101-1-119](https://doi.org/10.1210/endo-101-1-119). PMID: 862551.
-   Chegini S et al. Direct enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and a radioimmunoassay for melatonin compared. *Clinical Chemistry*. 1995. PMID: 7882512.

Focus on findings that affect the validity, interpretation or practical conduct of melatonin measurement. Compare studies where relevant and distinguish well-supported findings from common practice or convention.

#### Sources of variability and uncertainty

**Suggested length: 100-150 words.** Identify the main biological, behavioral, technical or analytical factors that could explain variation between participants, studies or methods. Note important limitations, unresolved questions and situations in which the available evidence may not generalize.

#### Implications for measurement and reporting

**Suggested length: 100-150 words.** Translate the evidence into consequences for study design and conduct. State what researchers should control, standardize, measure, document or report, and explain briefly why these elements matter.

#### Protocol recommendation

**Maximum 80 words.** Give a concise recommendation that can be incorporated directly into the final cohort melatonin protocol. It should be specific enough to act on and should distinguish requirements supported by evidence from pragmatic choices that simply need to be standardized within a study.

#### References

Provide **5-8 references in total**, including the seed literature and at least **2 additional papers identified independently**. Include DOI and PMID whenever available, with the DOI formatted as a clickable link.
